text.p: The following are the main stories from Thursday morning's German newspapers:
FRANKFURTER ALLGEMEINE ZEITUNG
- Germany's budget deficit was higher than planned in 1996 at 18.4 billion marks, Finance Minister Theo Waigel says.
- Inflation at lowest level for years, latest figures from Federal Statistics Office show.
- Prosecutors say recent killings of two young girls could be connected.
- Financial situation of Germany's communes improves slightly in 1996.
- Economic institutes call for economic initiatives in former communist east to be made more efficient.
- Labour Minister Norbert Bluem hints parts of planned rise in value-added tax could be used to help finance social security system.
HANDELSBLATT
- Opposition Social Democrats (SPD) say record 1996 deficit means 1996 budget was anti-constitutional.
- Doubts cast over future of Transrapid high-speed rail link between Berlin and Hamburg after Transport Minister Matthias Wissmann says project is not guaranteed "at any price".
- Capital trading tax to be abolished at start of 1998 at the earliest, finance ministry official says.
- Continental AG plans to cut salaries for new employees by 10 percent starting in 1998.
SUEDDEUTSCHE ZEITUNG
- Lower Saxony state premier Gerhard Schroeder, a leading member of the SPD, calls for a five-year freeze on tax rises.
- Agriculture and food industries expect increase in turnover of between one and two percent in 1997 and remain generally sceptical about their prospects.
- Russian presidential hopeful Alexander Lebed says on visit to Bonn that collapse of Russia could lead to a third world war.
DIE WELT
- Compromise in sight over how planned rise in value-added tax should be used, sources in coalition parties say.
- Turkish community leaders report "panic" at government plans to introduce visas for foreign children.
- Bond and stock markets reach new record levels.
- Bernhard Jagoda, president of Federal Labour Office, presents action plan aimed at creating 2.5 million new jobs by the year 2005.
